facts.text: The pink-eared duck has a large spatulate bill like the Australasian shoveler, but is smaller at 38–40 cm in length.
facts.quote: The pink-eared duck has a large spatulate bill like the Australasian shoveler, but is smaller at 38–40 cm length.

facts.text: Its brown back and crown, black and white barred sides and black eye patches on an otherwise white face make the bird unmistakable.
facts.quote: Its brown back and crown, black and white barred sides and black eye patches on its otherwise white face make this bird unmistakable.

facts.text: The pink 'ear' that gives the duck its name is only noticeable at close distance.
facts.quote: Its vernacular name refers to a pink spot in the corner formed by the black head pattern; it is only noticeable at close distance however

facts.text: The pink-eared duck feeds on plankton, crustaceans, mollusks and insects.
facts.quote: They are dependent on plankton, as well as crustaceans, mollusks and insects.

facts.text: Two pink-eared ducks sometimes feed by vortexing, spinning around a central point to concentrate food in a gyrating water column.
facts.quote: They also feed by vortexing, in which two ducks spin about a central point with the head of one opposite the tail of the other, concentrating food in a gyrating water column.

facts.text: In good years, large numbers of pink-eared ducks gather in shallow flood plains to nest.
facts.quote: In good years, large numbers of pink-eared ducks concentrate in shallow flood plains.

facts.text: The species can appear anywhere in Australia with standing water, especially in dry inland regions.
facts.quote: Widely distributed throughout Australia and highly mobile, these ducks can appear anywhere there is standing water, especially in dry inland regions

facts.text: It is the only member of the order Anseriformes known to have carotenoid pigments in its feathers.
facts.quote: This species is the only member of the order Anseriformes known to have carotenoid pigments in its feathers, in the characteristic pink "ear" spot.

facts.text: An X-ray study in Victoria found that between 6% and 19% of all hunted ducks live with embedded shot pellets in their bodies.
facts.quote: An X-ray study of ducks caught using nets in Victoria found that between 6% and 19% of all hunted ducks live with embedded shot pellets in their bodies.
